title: TB5-03291
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX (the Appellants) allege to be citizens of Somalia and appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claims for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX (the Appellants) allege to be citizens of Somalia and appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claims for refugee protection. XXXX XXXX is the designated representative for XXXX XXXX, a minor. They have submitted new evidence in support of their appeal and request an oral hearing. The Appellants ask the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to grant their appeal and confer them refugee status. In the alternative, the Appellants ask the RAD to refer the matter back to the RPD for a new hearing.

This appeal is allowed. Pursuant to Section 111(1)(c) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD refers the matter to the RPD for re-determination by a differently-constituted panel. Background

XXXX XXXX alleged before the RPD that she feared for her life in Somalia as a Yibir woman married to a man from a majority tribe. She also alleged a fear that her daughter, XXXX XXXX, would be subjected to female genital mutilation.

The Appellants' applications for refugee protection were heard on October 16, 2014. By a decision of November 20, 2014 the RPD rejected the claims finding that the Appellants had failed to provide credible evidence that, on a balance of probabilities, established their identities, their citizenships, the places where they resided prior to their arrival in Canada, the dates of departure and arrival, their tribal affiliation and the existence of a mixed marriage.

The Appellants submit that the RPD erred in failing to properly apply the Gender Guidelines,1 failing to provide an opportunity to respond to credibility concerns, making an improper plausibility finding, and ignoring and misconstruing relevant evidence. ANALYSIS Role of the RAD

What is the role of the RAD in considering an appeal against a decision of the RPD? The Appellants submit that the hybrid approach arising from the Huruglica2 decision is the more appropriate approach in their context, given the RAD's authority to consider new documents and to make its own determination.

The RAD notes that in Huruglica the Court considered the appropriate relationship between the RAD and the RPD. It found that the RAD had erred in simply reviewing the RPD's decision on a standard of reasonableness, rather than conducting its own independent assessment of the Appellants' refugee claims. The Court held that the RAD's application of a reasonableness standard curtailed the tribunal's appellate role, contrary to the purpose of the RAD and the provisions of IRPA. In the Court's view, the RAD should not even engage in a standard of review analysis; rather, it should consider the purpose of the appellate tribunal, the statutory provisions, comparable expertise, and comparative appellate regimes.3

Justice Phelan stated the following in Huruglica: Having concluded that the RAD erred in reviewing the RPD's decision on the standard of reasonableness, I have further concluded that for the reasons above, the RAD is required to conduct a hybrid appeal. It must review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the claimant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Where its assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own decision.4 In conducting its assessment, it can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion but it is not restricted, as an appellate court is, to intervening on facts only where there is an "overriding and palpable error."5

Considering the Court's decision in Huruglica, the RAD will review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of the Appellant's refugee claim, recognizing and respecting the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion. Where the RAD's assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD will substitute its own determination. Admissibility of New Evidence

Section 110(4) of the IRPA provides that the Appellants may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claims or that was not reasonably available, or that they could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection. It is for the Appellants to make full and detailed submissions in their Memorandum about how any proposed new evidence meets the requirements of section 110(4) and how that evidence relates to them.6

The Appellants have tendered two documents as proposed new evidence in support of their appeal. The first document is a copy of XXXX XXXX marriage certificate7 and the second document is a copy of an e-mail message from XXXX XXXX to her counsel.8

The Appellants submit that the documents proposed as new evidence meet the requirements of section 110(4) of the IRPA as they were not reasonably available at the time of the rejection of their claims. They explain that XXXX XXXX had spoken to her husband prior to the hearing and asked him to send her the marriage certificate, but he did not do so. It was only when she spoke to him after the rejection decision and described the urgency of the situation that her husband agreed to take the risk to obtain the document. The Appellants further explain that XXXX XXXX could not control her husband's decision-making and she made best efforts to obtain the document at an earlier date, but those efforts only proved successful more recently.

The RAD notes XXXX XXXX testimony at her hearing before the RPD. She indicated that she had asked her husband to send her marriage papers but he had left the papers behind when they fled Jigjiga. The RAD also notes XXXX XXXX explanation that she could not control her husband's decision-making with respect to taking a risk to travel to Jigjiga to obtain the marriage papers. As such, the RAD finds that the Appellants have demonstrated that the documents proposed as new evidence were not reasonably available at the time of the rejection of their claims and will be accepted as new evidence in this appeal.9 Application for an Oral Hearing
The Appellants ask that an oral hearing be held, pursuant to Section 110(6) of the IRPA.10

Section 110(3) of IRPA requires that the RAD proceed without a hearing, on the basis of the RPD record, while allowing the RAD to accept documentary evidence and submissions from the Minister and the Appellant. The person, who is the subject of the appeal may, pursuant to Section 110(4), present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.

According to Section 110(6), upon which the Appellants rely, the RAD may hold a hearing if, in its opinion, there is documentary evidence referred to in 110(3) that raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellant, that is central to the RPD's decision, and that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim. In this appeal, where there is no evidence from or in response to the Minister, the documentary evidence referred to in Section 110(3) must be understood in relation to Section 110(4).

When read together, Sections 110(3), (4), and (6) establish that the RAD must not hold a hearing in an appeal such as this unless there is new (Section 110(4)) evidence, in which case the RAD may hold a hearing if that new evidence raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellant, is central to the RPD's decision, and that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.

The Appellants submit that the new evidence noted above is central to the decision on their refugee protection claims and justifies allowing the claims. They argue that the new evidence serves to corroborate identity, which was a fundamental concern at the hearing. The Appellants submit that the new evidence confirms XXXX XXXX name, date of birth and place of birth, as well as her husband's name, date of birth and place of birth. They further submit that the new evidence corroborates the date and location of XXXX XXXX marriage. The Appellants argue that the marriage certificate also serves to strengthen the credibility of XXXX XXXX testimony, as the information provided on the document is entirely consistent with her oral and written testimony. They submit that the document raises a serious issue with respect to credibility. The Appellants submit that the RAD ought to hold a hearing to evaluate the new documentary evidence if their arguments, noted above, are not found to be sufficient on their own to overturn the RPD decision.

The RAD has reviewed the new evidence admitted in this appeal. It notes several anomalies on the face of the marriage certificate presented as new evidence. The letterhead of the Dawlada Deegaanka Soomalida is superimposed with another letterhead from the same entity. Furthermore, Supreme Court is misspelled on the letterhead and reads Islamic Sharea Suprme Court. Supreme Court is correctly spelled at the bottom of the certificate where it is indicated The Islamic sharea supreme court certify that this marriage is legal. The RAD notes that this statement contains grammatical errors and should correctly read The Islamic Sharea Supreme Court certifies that this marriage is legal. The marriage certificate is also not dated. Moreover, the marriage certificate presented as new evidence is not the original certificate. It was sent to the Appellant as an attachment to an e-mail message.

Considering the above, the RAD finds that the problems on the face of the copy of the marriage certificate cannot be addressed by the Appellants at a hearing since neither of them are the originator of the document. The RAD further finds that the new evidence, if accepted, would not justify allowing or rejecting the Appellants' refugee protection claims. As such, the RAD must proceed without a hearing and the Appellants' request for an oral hearing is denied.

The Appellants argue that the RPD erred in failing to properly apply the Gender Guidelines,11 failing to provide an opportunity to respond to credibility concerns, making an improper plausibility finding, and ignoring and misconstruing relevant evidence.

The RAD reviewed all the evidence in this case, including the recording of the Appellants' hearing before the RPD. From the recording, it was noted that during the hearing the RPD had concerns with respect to the Appellants' credibility, including the credibility of their identities, and presented them to XXXX XXXX for explanations. It was evident that the RPD had further concerns about XXXX XXXX explanations. It must be noted that the Appellants' hearing was conducted via videoconference with the Appellants and their counsel and witness located in Ottawa and the RPD and the interpreter located in Montreal. During the hearing, there were a number of interruptions to the video and audio feed of the videoconference as a result of technical difficulties. After each interruption, however the connection to the videoconference was restored.

During a pause in the proceeding, the interpreter comments to the RPD panel that XXXX XXXX looked very young. The RPD panel responds, "She claims to be XXXX years old". He goes on to say, "She could easily have been born in 1992 in Ethiopia". The comments concern the Appellants' credibility and identities. Although the comments appear to have been made while there was a break in the communication with the parties in Ottawa, the recorder continued to record in Montreal. Further evidence was adduced after these comments were made. The matter was on-going and not concluded when the RPD panel and the interpreter engaged in the dialog.

As a result, an issue before the RAD is whether the RPD's comments would cause a reasonable person informed of the facts to conclude that the RPD had pre-judged one of the Appellants, XXXX XXXX, such that she and her daughter did not receive a fair hearing. That is, was there a reasonable apprehension of bias? Although the Appellants did not raise this issue with the RPD or RAD, once the RAD became aware of the comments it was required to address it. Reasonable Apprehension of Bias

The principles of natural justice require that the procedures of the RPD be fair. In other words, the RPD must ensure that the procedures used before, during and after a hearing are fair in all the circumstances. Natural justice ensures that the refugee claimant has a chance to be heard and an opportunity to answer to the case being made against him or her. The refugee claimant must also have an independent and impartial decision-maker decide his or her case. The decision-maker must not have formed a preconceived decision and must not have a personal interest in the outcome of the case. Credibility cannot be prejudged; it must be determined based on the particular circumstances of the case.

The rule against bias is one of the main rules of natural justice which provides that the refugee claimant is entitled to have an independent and impartial decision-maker decide the case. The rule against bias is a common law rule that expresses the fundamental principle of natural justice that 'no man ought to be a judge in his own cause'. The rule against bias disqualifies a decision-maker from determining any case in which there is actual bias or an appearance of bias, also described as a reasonable apprehension of bias.

The test for "reasonable apprehension of bias" was formulated in the Supreme Court of Canada case, Committee for Justice and Liberty v. National Energy Board,12 as follows: What would an informed person, viewing the matter realistically and practically - and having thought the matter through - conclude. Would he think that it is more likely than not that [the decision-maker], whether consciously or unconsciously, would not decide fairly.

The Federal Court of Appeal stated the following in Satiacum:13 The opinion of de Grandpré J., dissenting, in Committee for Justice and Liberty et al. v. National Energy Board et al., [1978] 1 S.C.R. 369 has been accepted in this country as expressing the modern test for determining the existence of a reasonable apprehension of bias. Adopting the formulation proposed by this Court, he said (at pages 394-395):

The proper test to be applied in a matter of this type was correctly expressed by the Court of Appeal. As already seen by the quotation above, the apprehension of bias must be a reasonable one, held by reasonable and right-minded persons, applying themselves to the question and obtaining thereon the required information. In the words of the Court of Appeal, that test is "what would an informed person, viewing the matter realistically and practically - and having thought the matter through - conclude. Would he think that it is more likely than not that [the decision-maker], whether consciously or unconsciously, would not decide fairly."

I can see no real difference between the expressions found in the decided cases, be they 'reasonable apprehension of bias', 'reasonable suspicion of bias', or 'real likelihood of bias'. The grounds for this apprehension must, however, be substantial and I entirely agree with the Federal Court of Appeal which refused to accept the suggestion that the test be related to the "very sensitive or scrupulous conscience".
In Newfoundland Telephone Co., the Supreme Court restated this test as follows: "whether a reasonably informed bystander could reasonably perceive bias on the part of an adjudicator".14

Thus, the impartiality of decision-makers is not judged from the decision-maker's perspective, but from that of a reasonable bystander, fully informed of all relevant facts. For example, certain activities and associations of a member may seem quite inconsequential from the member's perspective, and yet still appear highly suspect from an observer's point of view.

As stated by the Supreme Court of Canada in Arsenault-Cameron v. Prince Edward Island, "The test for apprehension of bias takes into account the presumption of impartiality. A real likelihood of bias must be demonstrated."15 The Supreme Court reiterated this principle in Wewaykum: "The standard refers to an apprehension of bias that rests on serious grounds, in light of the strong presumption of judicial impartiality."16
The principles and considerations noted above are equally applicable to administrative tribunals, which are presumed to be impartial in their decision-making.17

Nevertheless, if there is an allegation that the member displayed bias, for example, because he or she prejudged the claim, the Court will require clear evidence that a predetermination had in fact occurred. The Federal Court reiterated in Ali18 that: [4]... the Court of Appeal in Arthur v. Canada (Attorney General), [2001] F.C.J. No. 1091 [(F.C.A., no. A-991-90), MacGuigan, Linden, Gray, November 2, 1992, reported: 18 Imm. L.R. (2d) 22 (F.C.A.)], has emphasized that an allegation of bias cannot be done lightly. It cannot rest on mere suspicion, pure conjecture or mere impressions of an applicant. It must be supported by material evidence.

Moreover, as the Supreme Court noted in R. v. S. (R.D.):19 True impartiality does not require that the judge have no sympathies or opinions; it requires that the judge nevertheless be free to entertain and act upon different points of view with an open mind. The Court noted that "a mere suspicion is not enough" to support an allegation of bias.

Considering the case law, it is clear that a reasonable apprehension of bias is sufficient to disqualify a member from deciding a case. Regardless of whether a member is consciously or unconsciously biased, or even unbiased, what matters is whether a reasonable, informed person looking fairly at all of the facts, would conclude that the member would not decide fairly. A reasonable apprehension of bias is sufficient to disqualify a panel from deciding a case even if the panel member is confident that he or she can act impartially. However, this must be supported by material evidence.

In this case, it is clear that the RPD made comments, mid-hearing, related to the matter which was being considered. The comment was made in the context of the RPD's adjudicative function. The RPD reaches a conclusion with respect to the Appellants' credibility prior to hearing responses to all questions posed to one of the Appellants (XXXX XXXX), including responses to her counsel's questions during her examination. The RPD drew a conclusion with respect to the Appellants' credibility prior to their counsel being given the opportunity to explain or otherwise qualify any damaging testimony. In the case of Sheferaw,20 the Federal Court found that the RPD's oral decision implied that a decision had been reached prior to the close of the hearing. The RPD must not have the appearance of having already decided the case before hearing all the evidence even though the hearing might not have brought anything new.

In the case of Paulino,21 the Federal Court held that the Immigration Appeal Division decision as a whole was highly influenced by the member's discovery that the applicant and her spouse had lied and fabricated evidence for the visitor's visa application. Her attitude and approach is that, because they lied once, nothing they now say about the genuineness of their marriage can be believed and that, indeed, the authenticity of the copious documentation that the couple produced on point is also fatally undermined. The focus on the visitor's visa situation to the exclusion of just about everything else suggests a closed mind and evinces a reasonable apprehension of bias which led to an unreasonable decision.

In the case at hand, the RPD expressed an opinion on the merits of the Appellants' claims during their hearing. The RPD expressed a view that suggests a predisposition to decide the case a certain way. There is evidence of prejudgement in the comments made by the RPD. As such, the RAD finds that the RPD's comments, noted above, would cause a reasonable person informed of the facts to conclude that the RPD had pre-judged the conduct of one of the Appellants such that she and her daughter did not receive a fair hearing. The RAD finds that there was a reasonable apprehension of bias on the part of the RPD. Disposition

As set out above, the RAD has found that there was a reasonable apprehension of bias on the part of the RPD in rejecting the Appellants' claims. The Appellants ask the RAD to grant their appeal and confer them refugee status. The RAD is not able to satisfy this request as the RPD decision must be void. As noted in Newfoundland Telephone Co. v. Newfoundland, once a court has determined that there has been a reasonable apprehension of bias, the decision in question must be void.22 The RAD cannot confer the Appellants' refugee status without hearing evidence that was presented to the RPD. As there were problems identified with the new evidence that was presented to the RAD and the RAD found that it did not justify allowing the Appellants' refugee protection claims, the RAD cannot hold an oral hearing.

The RAD is in a position to grant the Appellants their alternate request to refer the matter back to the RPD for a new hearing. As a result of the finding of a reasonable apprehension of bias, this appeal is allowed and the matter is referred back to the RPD for a full re-hearing of the Appellants' refugee protection claims.
Pursuant to Section 111(1)(c) of IRPA, the RAD refers the matter to the RPD for redetermination by a differently-constituted panel.

This appeal is therefore allowed. (signed) "M. Pettinella" M.
